utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here and the presentation is exactly as it was yesterday, except for some legal assistants. Mr. Bourgon, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning to all my colleagues in the courtroom. On the screen before you, if you flick -- if you press the button for e-court, you see "The Boring Figure" which I was referring to yesterday. Surprisingly, when she failed to appear on the screen yesterday because I forgot to ask the Registrar to press on the e-court button, nobody reacted, so I take it that everyone was concentrating too much on what I had to say. In any event, what I said yesterday, Mr. President, is that whether you see the old lady with the sad look and her chin in the lower part of the picture or whether you see the young lady with her fur coat and looking to the rear, what does matter is that if you put your mind to it, you will see the second lady in this picture and she will reveal herself to you. Well, the same goes for the Prosecution's case. If you put your mind to it, and I'm sure you will, and you disregard all of the unreliable evidence which cannot be attributed any probative value, it will become clear to you that the Prosecution failed to prove its case against Drago Nikolic. That being said, Mr. President, it has become clear to me, based on the number of pages I covered yesterday in 50 minutes, that I will simply not be able to cover all the material my team and I had prepared, so I have no choice but to skip many topics, and I'll try to focus solely on what is indispensable. These are the topics I will cover today, and they appear on the screen before you. My colleague will then conclude our closing arguments by addressing the Trial Chamber in respect of character evidence and sentencing considerations. If I can move into private session, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Next on my list is Momir Nikolic. I refer the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 589 to 646 in the Nikolic final trial brief. Our submission concerning Momir Nikolic is that no probative value can be attributed to his testimony that he visited the Zvornik Brigade Command and the Zvornik Brigade IKM in the evening of 13 July 1995. Despite the fact that Momir Nikolic has become another professional witness who knows his narrative by heart and who has been repeating it in many trials, when testifying before this courtroom, before this Trial Chamber, he made at least two obvious factual mistakes. He stated that when he arrived at the Zvornik Brigade on 13 July, in the evening, he parked his car outside, he came in by foot. He identified himself as Momir Nikolic. He said he wanted to see Drago Nikolic, and he said he was a security organ of the Bratunac Brigade. All of this, Mr. President, are not -- is not something which Witness Jeremic could miss. Jeremic actually confirmed in his statement, that is 3D587, that it simply did not take place. Significantly, the Prosecution did not challenge the statement which was admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Another significant mistake made by Momir Nikolic is that when he testified that he did not go in the IKM when he allegedly spoke to Drago Nikolic or as he testified to the contrary in the Blagojevic trial, transcript 33251/33525. Again, this is something he could not forget. It is evident that Momir Nikolic was but attempting to shape his testimony to avoid answering questions that he would not be able to answer concerning the Zvornik Brigade IKM because he never went there. Next slide, please. Such mistakes, considered along with our detailed arguments, demonstrate that his testimony regarding this alleged visit cannot be attributed any weight. That being said, Mr. President, there are parts of his testimony which must be attributed some weight. One such issue is the following: Momir Nikolic testified about the chaos and the improvisation in Bratunac on the night of 13 July, when orders and counter-orders were being issued by the minute concerning the prisoners; transcript 33233/33234. This is significant, as it illustrates the lack of any existing plan as to what was going to happen to the prisoners at least up to that point. Next slide, please. Next on my list is Vinko Pandurevic; Nikolic final trial brief 956 to 1015. As a preliminary matter, I wish to state for the record that our submissions are not related in any way to the alleged responsibility of Vinko Pandurevic for the events of July 1995. This is way beyond our purpose. However, insofar as we are convinced that Vinko Pandurevic did not tell the truth when he testified before this Trial Chamber, and that this testimony directly affected the situation of our client in this case, then this cannot be ignored. It is our position that the evidence he provided concerning his alleged meeting with Dragan Obrenovic on 16 July at the IKM, during which Obrenovic would have informed him for the first time about the presence of prison ers in the area of Zvornik, and his knowledge of their fate, cannot be attributed any probative value. The evidence reveals that Pandurevic was informed of the details of the prisoner situation by Obrenovic, whether at the Zvornik Brigade Command or at the IKM, or in both places, as of 15 July 1995. What is most important is that Pandurevic was informed of this situation before 16 July. When Pandurevic was informed by Obrenovic of the details of the prisoner situation, it is our submission, Mr. President, that Obrenovic did not tell him that he obtained this information from Drago Nikolic. Had Pandurevic been informed that Obrenovic obtained this information from Drago Nikolic, he would necessarily have engaged Nikolic on this matter, exactly as he testified, that he would have expected Obrenovic to confirm the order he was allegedly informed of by Drago Nikolic. Quite to the contrary, Pandurevic confirmed that he did not speak to Drago Nikolic on 15 July; transcript 31513. More importantly, when Pandurevic reacted to the detailed information he received from Obrenovic on 15 July - that's when he sent his interim combat report - he did not involve Drago Nikolic, who was the Zvornik Brigade duty officer, in any way; transcript 31585/31586. Pandurevic would have contacted Drago Nikolic if he had been involved in the way Obrenovic suggested. This confirms that Drago Nikolic was no more than a minor player in these events. Lastly, we also fully agree with the Prosecution's submission that the theory put forward by Pandurevic, that he did not exercise effective control over all elements of the Zvornik Brigade when returning to Zvornik on 15 July, makes no sense. The evidence speaks for itself in this -- on this issue. A quick word must be said also about Pandurevic, who made it very clear how much he disliked the security branch, in general, as well as Drago Nikolic, in particular. Why? Because of the information that Drago Nikolic would have reported about him. The fact of the matter is, Mr. President, that this apparent conflict, if I may use this word, between Pandurevic and Drago Nikolic is unrelated to the events of July 1995. Next slide, please. Next on my list is PW-101. For the reasons set out in our brief, paragraphs 845 to 891, it is our submission that the evidence provided by this witness cannot be attached any weight. The evidence reveals that PW-101 did go to Orahovac in the evening of 14 July, but he was never ordered by Sreten Milosevic to take food to the execution site, and he never went there. In light of the detailed submissions provided by my colleague Zivanovic on Monday - transcript 34372/34377 - there's no need for me to add anything else concerning this witness. PW-101 clearly had a reason to provide such information to the Prosecution, and his testimony must be disregarded entirely. Next, Sreco Acimovic. For all the reasons set out in our final trial briefs, paragraphs 892 to 955, it is our submission that the entire testimony of this witness cannot be given any weight whatsoever. My colleague stated, and I quote -- that is, the Prosecution, that: "Acimovic is guilty and that he was in this up to his eyeballs." Transcript 34254. On this basis alone, his testimony should be set aside entirely. Time being of the essence, I move to the next witness. Wits PW-102 and PW-108, I refer the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 699 to 844 of the Nikolic final trial brief. It is our submission that the evidence provided by these two witnesses cannot be attached any probative value. Significantly, the Prosecution brief speaks for itself concerning the weight to be given to this evidence, four paragraphs, 2730 to 2733. In fact, it really appears as though the Prosecution decided to rely on the evidence of these two witnesses, knowing that it was not worthy of belief, with the aim of keeping the Defence team of Drago Nikolic busy. Well, that strategy worked. I can tell you that, Mr. President. Anything to salvage the testimony of PW-168. In the end, however, on the basis of our detailed arguments, there can be no doubt that the alleged visit of these witnesses to the Zvornik Command on the 14th of July never took place. I know that the Prosecution concurs that this visit could only have taken place on 14 July, which is one of the reasons why it simply cannot have taken place. I also take this opportunity to underscore the link between the narrative of Witness PW-168 and the evidence provided by PW-102 and PW-108. We take the view that this is yet another indication of the lack of credibility of Witness PW-168. Lastly, I turn to Mihajlo Galic. In the Nikolic final trial brief, paragraphs 647 to 698, it is our submission that no weight can be attributed to his testimony that he replaced Drago Nikolic at the IKM in the evening of 13 July. This -- in its final trial brief, the Prosecution challenged the credibility of Witness Dragan Stojkic, as well as the Defence assertion that the IKM operation duty officer log-book was tampered with. As for Witness Stojkic, his testimony regarding the time he spent with Tactical Group 1 and his return to the Zvornik Brigade is plausible and can be reconciled with the testimony of Jevdjevic and Dragutinovic, whom the Prosecution does not believe [indiscernible]. Stojkic may have been mistaken concerning the location where he spent the nights of 11 and 12 July, after Tactical Group 1 had entered Srebrenica, but there is no evidence contradicting his testimony that he was with the tank company that returned to Zvornik on 13 July. Using the standard which the Prosecution would like you to use in rejecting the testimony of Stojkic, this would result in the testimony of most witnesses in this case being rejected. Turning to the IKM log-book, the Prosecution fails to understand our arguments set out at paragraphs 680 to 697 of our final trial brief. Simply put, Mr. President, our submission is that the reason why the IKM duty officer log-book is, indeed, perfect regarding the number of pages in the book, regarding the numbering of the pages, regarding the stamp at the end with Obrenovic's signature on it certifying the number of pages, is precisely because it was tampered with. The IKM log-book is the only one of its category which was not transferred to the 5th Corps along with the Zvornik Brigade archives before the Prosecution conducting its search of those premises. This is not a coincidence. Obrenovic kept this book because it was part of his defence, and he wanted the Prosecution to have it. One last observation needs to be made in this regard, which is simply that if you look at this book, and if you look at the other entries made by Drago Nikolic in other books, it is simply not possible that the IKM -- that when Drago Nikolic was at the IKM on 13 July, which is undisputed, that he made no entry whatsoever in this book. Where did these entries go? Answering the question -- asking the question is providing the answer. Before moving on to my next topic, I take this opportunity to quickly address the evidence of Witnesses PW-143, Lazar Ristic, and I think it's 3D1, but it's a witness who testified in closed session. Regarding PW-143, we did not make any submission concerning his credibility in the Nikolic final trial brief. To put it simply, his testimony was so equivocal concerning the presence of Drago Nikolic at the Zvornik Brigade Command and at the school in Orahovac on the evening of 13 of July that it simply cannot be attributed any weight. I take this opportunity to add that it is our respectful submission that the questions put to him in redirect examination were impermissible. I refer you to Archbold, 2006, page 394. Moving on to Prosecution Lazar Ristic, the Prosecution suddenly argues something which my colleague repeated during his oral argument - transcript 34254 - that he was a major player along with members of his battalion, the 4th Battalion, and the executions which took place in Orahovac. This is not what the evidence reveals. This was never suggested during the testimony of Lazar Ristic before this Trial Chamber. I note in this regard that when he testified, the Prosecution did not even request that Lazar Ristic be given a Rule 90 Echo warning. The only reason for the Prosecution's unfair and inappropriate submission is that the evidence of Lazar Ristic establishes clearly that information provided to him by Witness PW-168 is a complete fabrication. If we can go in private session, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please, for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I immediately move on to my next topic, which is the missing evidence in this record. My colleague Ostojic has underscored the fact that the Prosecution refrained from calling many witnesses whose testimony was critical in order to fully establish what really happened in July 1995. I join his submission, and I draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the following witnesses who should have been called by the Prosecution: In particular, we respectfully submit, considering that the Trial Chamber met with Jasikovac, the commander of the Military Police Company, that it is unacceptable that he was not called by the Prosecution. Even though Jasikovac refused to meet with the Defence, we are convinced that his testimony could have allowed to confirm that Obrenovic is the one who personally received the information concerning the impending arrival of prisoners in the area of Zvornik; that Drago Nikolic was not contacted regarding this, and that Obrenovic is the one who issued the orders to Jasikovac to deploy to Orahovac with some members of the Military Police Company, members who, by the way, were not "hors de combat" or unfit for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt, but I don't -- the suggestion that the Trial Chamber met with Jasikovac, I'm not sure that's what you mean to say, and that, I'm not sure, should be in the record, line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague for this. I was talking about the Prosecution who met with Jasikovac. There was never any way that the Trial Chamber would be with Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you. Thank you, particularly Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As for Dragomir Vasic, he could have confirmed that Obrenovic never met with Jokic at Standard on the morning of 15 July. He could also have confirmed that Momir Nikolic was not privy to the alleged conversation between Deronjic and Beara on the night of 13 July. Lastly, considering that the Prosecution has withdrawn Witnesses Salapura and Golic from its Rule 65 ter list of witnesses, it is our submission that it cannot rely on entries in the Zvornik Brigade operations duty officer notebook involving Salapura and Golic to infer that Drago Nikolic worked closely with Beara and Popovic during the period from 13 to 16 July. This is not what the evidence reveals. After 14 July, Drago Nikolic clearly kept away from everything that was happening. Clearly, the Prosecution has never been interested in establishing the true involvement of Drago Nikolic if these events. I move to my next topic, the first joint criminal enterprise alleged by the Prosecution, forcible transfer. There are two preliminary issues I must deal with; namely, the victims who were supposedly forced out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves and the Prosecution's burden of proof pursuant to the JCE mode of liability. Regarding the victims of forcible transfer, this is an issue that arose during the presentation of arguments pursuant to Rule 98 bis. The Trial Chamber decided at that time that this was an issue best left to be determined at the final stage of the trial. Our position, set out in detail in the Nikolic final trial brief, is the following: The men who were separated from the crowd in Potocari, who were detained and transported to Bratunac, and the men who voluntarily left the Srebrenica enclave, only to be later captured as part of the column heading towards Tuzla, and they were then transported to Bratunac, both of these categories of men were not victims of forcible transfer. The Prosecution argues that these men were part of the Muslim population and that they were the victims of forcible transfer because they were lawfully present in Srebrenica. The Prosecution also suggests that these men did not exercise a genuine choice to leave the enclave and that they did so in order to escape the VRS attack on the enclave. That is paragraph 2897 of the Prosecution's brief. The Prosecution's arguments are erroneous, both in law and in fact. Without repeating all of our arguments: Firstly, what the Prosecution omits to consider is that in addition to the legal status of the men, an issue which we argue in our brief, what matters is what the alleged perpetrators intended to do with these men and the manner in which they were treated. Looking at the men who were separated from the women, children, and elderly in Potocari, it is evident that they were separated because the VRS intended to do something different with them that they did that they were not doing with the women, children, and elderly. The aim may have been or may not have been to forcibly transfer the women, children, and elderly. Not so for the men, however. If, as the Prosecution alleges, the decision to kill these men had already been taken, which is a conclusion we dispute, of course, then it was not forcible transfer. The crime envisaged was murder. On the other hand, if the decision had not been taken to kill these men, which is the conclusion we say the evidence supports, again detaining men who allegedly participated in hostilities, to screen them, and to treat them as prisoners, with a view to using them for a future exchange, is not forcible transfer. The Prosecution argues that the VRS did not view them as prisoners because they were not distinguishable as soldiers; paragraph 2907 of their brief. It is necessary to recall, as I did yesterday, that this was a non-international armed conflict, that these were men of fighting age, and that they were detained because of their suspected participation in hostilities against the VRS. The Prosecution also says that these men were denied food and water and that some were beaten, which implies that the VRS did not view them as prisoners. Of course, depriving prisoners of food and water and mistreating them, if that was established, is a violation of International Humanitarian Law, but it does not change the fact that these men were detained and were in the hands of the VRS at the time until it could be decided what to do with them. That is not forcible transfer. The fact that they were prisoners in the hands of the VRS allowed the VRS to transport them legitimately as prisoners to detention facilities, again which is not forcible transfer. What about the men who left for the column? Well, the most important consideration here is the fact that they left Srebrenica voluntarily. The evidence reveals that this was an organised withdrawal, the aim of which was for the members of the 28th Division and other men of fighting age to reach Tuzla, where they could assist the 2nd Corps of the ABiH in future combat operations. Contrary to the Prosecution's argument, these men were not forced to leave the Srebrenica enclave. The VRS had not even reached Srebrenica when the column started on its way to Tuzla. Pandurevic explained during his testimony that the 28th Division was retreating faster than he was advancing with Tactical Group 1. They weren't retreating. They were on their way to Tuzla already. Moreover, these men had the option at that time to surrender. The reference for Pandurevic here was 30867/30868. These men had the option to surrender. There was not -- there was at that time no prospects that they would be the object of criminal acts if they surrendered. Moreover, once the VRS realised that these men had left Srebrenica and that they were on their way to Tuzla, their immediate reaction was to intercept these men and to prevent them from reaching Tuzla, which shows that the VRS did not have forcible transfer in mind. If forcible transfer is what the VRS had in mind, they would have simply let the men reach Tuzla. Furthermore, once these men were captured along the road leading towards Konjevic Polje, the same reasoning applies as for the men who were separated in Potocari. If it was already decided to kill them, then -- which is not supported by the evidence, in our view, then it was not forcible transfer; it was murder. If the decision had not been made to kill these men, which is what we say the evidence supports, again detaining men who allegedly participated in hostilities and who are attempting to link up with their own forces, and transporting them to Bratunac and ultimately to Zvornik, is not forcible transfer. Consequently, it is evident, on the basis of the evidence on the record, that the men who were captured when travelling with the column, and the men who were separated, were not forcibly transferred out of Srebrenica. What about the men from Zepa? Time being of the essence, I will not address this issue, although I'd be glad to answer any questions in this -- on this topic. It follows, Mr. President, that the men who were separated in Potocari and the men who were -- who left Srebrenica with the column, were not forcibly transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but perhaps while you are still on forcible transfer, you could address the question of when this crime is consummated, is executed; is completed, in other words. In other words, whether arrival at a particular destination is required or whether it is completed at the same time that the persons are forcibly removed from where is their habitual residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The moment that the VRS detained the men who were separated from the crowd in Potocari, the crime which started then, if there was a crime, is detention or murder, or no crime at all, and it was not forcible transfer. As for the men from the column, the moment they left Srebrenica voluntarily, there was no forcible transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As will be argued later, even if the Trial Chamber would hold that these men were victims of forcible transfer, then there can be no doubt that the result would be the same for Drago Nikolic. Moving on to the second preliminary issue, the following are the essential elements of a JCE as a mode of liability. This is what the Prosecution must prove: First of all, of course, the mens rea, and that is on the screen before you; the intent to achieve a common purpose. The Prosecution must prove the applicable mens rea -- must determine the applicable mens rea for each of the crimes, the common purpose involved. This includes proof of any specific mental element required, such as the "Chapeau" requirement for crimes against humanity. The Prosecution must establish also that the components of the mens rea -- sorry, that the mens rea for each of the crimes has been established. If the Prosecution fails to prove any of these elements, then the accused is not a member of the joint criminal enterprise, in which case the criminal responsibility of the accused must be assessed pursuant to other modes of liability under Article 7(1) of the Statute. This is what we argue in the case of both JCEs for Drago Nikolic. Drago Nikolic did not have the required mens rea, which implies that he was not a member of the alleged -- of the two alleged JCEs. At his level, he never got the information about the two JCEs, and he was never a member. That is why his responsibility must be assessed pursuant to other modes of liability included in Article 7(1) of the Statute. Second, of course, the Prosecution must prove the actus reus which requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused significantly contributed to the accomplishment of the common purpose. Taking a closer look at the mens rea requirement for JCE, these are the steps on the screen before you which must be followed in order to determine whether the Prosecution has met its burden of prove. First, a common purpose must be identified precisely. Then it must be proved that the accused knew the common purpose. Third, it must be established beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to further the common purpose. The mens rea for each crime must be identified, and it must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused had the required mens rea for each of these crimes. The Prosecution uses the JCE mode of liability against Drago Nikolic. It's very clearly why -- very clear why. He's only in Orahovac, but he's guilty for everything because by significantly contributing to one of the execution sites, then he can be found guilty of all of them, but the Prosecution omits to consider that for this to happen, he must be a member of the JCE. And being a member of the JCE imposes on the Prosecution a very high threshold of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Drago Nikolic had this mens rea, that he was in the planning, in the creation of this JCE. And in order for him to accept the JCE later on down the line, he must still know what the JCE is. He must intend to further that common purpose. Drago Nikolic never had this intention, never had this detailed knowledge. As argued in the Nikolic final trial brief, the common purpose of the JCE alleged by the Prosecution, the first JCE, chronologically, is the following: To force the Muslim population out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to areas outside the control of the RS from about 8 March to the end of August 1995; paragraph 49 of the indictment. The word "and" which is underlined, is important. The JCE alleged by the Prosecution includes both Srebrenica and Zepa. Even though the Trial Chamber previously held that whether there was one or two JCEs related to the forcible transfer of the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa, the Trial Chamber said that this was a matter for evidence at trial. We respectfully submit at this stage it is not open, Mr. President, to the Trial Chamber to modify the common purpose of the JCE as alleged by the Prosecution in the indictment. In any event, even if the Trial Chamber was to split Zepa and Srebrenica, in terms of making two JCEs, the result would be the same. Moving on, Mr. President, we respectfully submit that the Prosecution's allegation that the Muslim population was to be forced out to areas outside the control of the VRS must also be proved. The Prosecution claimed that this is not an element of the crime. That's irrelevant. Of course it's an element of the crime. But as the Prosecution concedes, it's an element which defines the common purpose of the alleged joint criminal enterprise. And if it defines the common purpose, then, of course, the accused must be aware of the common purpose and he must intend to further the common purpose, which includes the transfer to areas outside the control of the RS. It is our submission that Drago Nikolic was not aware of the common purpose of this alleged JCE and that he never intended to further the common purpose. Well, let's take a look at Srebrenica enclave. Clearly, Mr. President, the evidence reveals that Drago Nikolic was never informed of the common purpose to force out the Muslim population composed of the women, children, and elderly who went from Srebrenica to Potocari, from the Srebrenica enclave to areas outside the control of the RS. This was argued in our brief at paragraphs 1027 to 1043. Significantly, the Prosecution agrees with this submission at least for two reasons. First, they do not counter our submission that Drago Nikolic was never informed of the common purpose to force out the Muslim women, children, and elderly. Second, looking at paragraphs 2785 to 2787, the Prosecution refers specifically to the knowledge of Drago Nikolic concerning the prisoners or the men from Bratunac, never is anything mentioned about the women, children, and elderly in Potocari. Accordingly, if we are right in saying that only the Muslim women, children, and elderly were forcibly transferred, then the only conclusion is that Drago Nikolic did not have knowledge of this common purpose to force them out of the Srebrenica enclave. Due to time constraints, I will not address the Zepa enclave, which is addressed in our brief. Let me recall -- the only conclusion, then, Mr. President, is that the required mens rea to be a member of the JCE has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. Therefore, Drago Nikolic was not a member of that JCE. As mentioned earlier, this is of the utmost importance in considering the criminal responsibility of Drago Nikolic in relation to all the events which took place in the Srebrenica area in July 1995 and the related allegations in the indictment. Obviously, if Drago Nikolic was not a member of the JCE to forcibly transfer the Muslim population, this establishes a clear difference between Drago Nikolic and any person found to be a member of this JCE. Moving on, Mr. President, because we say he's not a member, it's not necessary to address the mens rea applicable to the crimes included in the JCE, but I would be glad to answer any questions on this issue. It's not necessary, either, to address whether he significantly contributed to this JCE, but I will not address this issue, either, but I will be glad to answer any questions. There is no -- the only possible conclusion, because he was not a member, and that there is no evidence and the Prosecution has proved -- has failed to prove, sorry, that Drago Nikolic incurs responsibility pursuant to either the JCE mode of liability or other modes of liability included under Article 7(1) of the Statute. He was not involved in any way in forcing the out the Muslim population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to areas outside the control of the RS. Now, the question is: What if the Trial Chamber rules that the men from Bratunac, in respect of the Srebrenica enclave, and the military-abled population in relation to the Zepa enclave, if the Trial Chamber rules that they are included in the persons who were forcibly transferred and deported, it is our submission that the result is the same. There is no evidence that if and when Drago Nikolic was informed of the arrival of prisoners in the area of Zvornik, he knew that these men were anything but prisoners. In any event, he did not know that these men -- how these men ended up in Bratunac. He did not have information about the separation of men in Potocari. He did not have information about men captured from the column. He did not have information how the men captured from the column were taken to Bratunac. The evidence reveals that what he knew, after allegedly meeting with Beara and Popovic on 14 July, is that he was tasked with accommodating some people coming for exchange purposes, something he was not previously informed of, and there were no mention of killings. When the question was put to my colleague whether he could point to any evidence that Drago Nikolic was informed that the prisoners who arrived in the Zvornik area had been forced out of the Srebrenica enclave, he was not able to identify any relevant evidence on the record; transcript 34264/34268. As also argued in our brief and as I said earlier, Mr. President, in response to your question, the crime of responsible transfer was over by the time these persons arrived in the Zvornik area. Also, with respect to the actus reus, it simply cannot be said that by directing the buses carrying these prisoners from the Hotel Vidikovac to one or more of the schools in Zvornik significantly contributed to forcing out these men out of the Srebrenica enclave to areas outside the control of the RS. It is also significant that these men were never transferred to areas outside the control of the RS which, as mentioned earlier, is an allegation which the Prosecution had to prove. As for the military men from the Zepa enclave, there is no evidence that Drago Nikolic was aware of the alleged crimes occurring in Zepa at the time, let alone that he ever intended to forcibly transfer these men to areas outside the control of the RS or to deport these men across a national border. For all of these reasons, Mr. President, Drago Nikolic must be acquitted of Counts 7 and 8. I move to the second JCE alleged by the Prosecution, starting once again with the identification of the precise common purpose. As argued in our final trial brief, the purpose of the JCE alleged by the Prosecution is the following: To kill all the able-bodied men -- Muslim men, sorry, from Srebrenica. The Prosecution did not dispute this submission during its oral arguments. What is significant here, Mr. President, is the word "all." The Prosecution cannot argue that the indictment means or implies a different common purpose. As argued at length in our brief, paragraphs 1149 to 1204, the evidence reveals that Drago Nikolic never knew of, nor that he was ever informed, about the common plan, design, or purpose to murder all the Muslim men or the able-bodied Muslim men from Srebrenica. The evidence adduced by the Prosecution fails to prove otherwise. I draw your attention to paragraph 1160 of our final trial brief. Even if the statement of facts provided by Obrenovic and/or Momir Nikolic were given any weight, contrary to our submissions, Dijan [phoen] would have learned, worst-case scenario, of a crime about to be committed against a large number of prisoners about to be transported to the area of Zvornik. Drago Nikolic did not know, and it is not possible to infer that he knew how many prisoners were to be transported to Zvornik, nor that he knew how these men ended up to Bratunac. Moreover, considering that Drago Nikolic was the duty officer at the IKM until 14 July, in the morning, it may possibly be inferred that he knew that a significant component of the 28th Division had already entered the area of Zvornik. Hence, when he was informed that prisoners were arriving or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When he was informed about the prisoners about to arrive in the Zvornik area, there is no way that he could assume that these prisoners represented all the men from Srebrenica. A large component were fighting in his own territory. It is our submission, Mr. President, that there is no evidence and that it cannot be inferred that Drago Nikolic was informed of the alleged common purpose to kill all the able-bodied men during the alleged meeting of 14 July when he supposedly met with Ljubisa Beara and Vujadin Popovic. There is no evidence that he was aware of the common purpose to kill all of the able-bodied men before attending this meeting. Secondly, the evidence provided by Bircakovic about his conversation with Drago Nikolic as he was coming out of this alleged meeting is credible and must be accorded full weight. Hence, there is direct evidence on the record that during this meeting, Drago Nikolic was not informed about the killing of prisoners, let alone about the common purpose to kill all of the able-bodied men from Srebrenica enclave. Moreover, even if Drago Nikolic would have been informed during this meeting that the prisoners about to arrive would be killed, this still falls short of the required knowledge of the common purpose for Drago to become a member of that joint criminal enterprise. It is necessary to recall that at that moment, Drago Nikolic knows that a significant number of able-bodied men from Srebrenica are fighting their way in the very area of Zvornik, and he may possibly have known that the orders coming from the Main Staff were to prevent these men from linking up with the 2nd Corps, not to kill them. The Prosecution advances that Beara and Popovic had no reason to lie to their fellow security officer by telling him that the prisoners were to be exchanged. Of course, we disagree with this proposition for many reasons. Firstly, even though Drago Nikolic was a security officer, and if such conversation ever took place, the Prosecution appears to place on an equal footing Drago Nikolic with senior officers of a much higher level. Drago Nikolic was but a security officer of a brigade. He had the lowest possible rank for an officer. Hence, there would be no reason for Beara and Popovic to share with Drago Nikolic the details of the common purpose, if it ever existed. What they would necessarily have been interested in would be giving instructions to Drago Nikolic as to what they expected of him; nothing more. That does not make Drago Nikolic a member of that JCE. Moreover, the Prosecution's argument that Beara and Popovic had no reason to lie can also apply to Drago Nikolic, who had no reason to lie to his fellow security officer, Slavko Peric from the 1st Battalion, or to his driver, Bircakovic. There is no evidence that Slavko Peric, Rajko Babic, Momir Pelemis, ever received any information, whether from the telegram they allegedly received or from Drago Nikolic, that the prisoners were to be killed, let alone that the aim was to kill all able-bodied men from Srebrenica. Hence, the Prosecution's submission implies that Bircakovic lied, Babic lied, Peric lied, and/or that Drago Nikolic lied to them. That's not supported by the evidence. Furthermore, even considering what the Prosecution submits Beara and Popovic would have told Drago Nikolic during this meeting, this does not include information related to the common purpose of the alleged JCE; i.e., to kill all able-bodied men from Srebrenica. Lastly, the Prosecution advances, during this meeting, that Drago Nikolic would have made proposals on suitable locations for detaining, executing, and burying and the prisoners about to arrive. This allegation is unsupported by any evidence. The fact that Drago Nikolic was a security officer and that he may have been familiar with the area of Zvornik is insufficient, in the absence of direct evidence as to what was actually discussed during this alleged meeting, to infer that he was aware of the common purpose. The same goes for the fact that Drago Nikolic -- sorry, for the fact that engineering equipment was deployed, or the fact that soon after this meeting, buses of prisoners arrive in the area of Zvornik. The ultimate question, Mr. President, is whether, on the basis of the evidence on the record, it can be inferred beyond a reasonable doubt that Drago Nikolic was informed by Beara and Popovic of the common purpose of the alleged JCE to kill all the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. This question, Mr. President, must be answered in the negative because, simply, there are other possibilities supported by the evidence. Then such an inference cannot be made. To mention but one such possibility, the evidence supports the inference that Drago Nikolic was called to attend a meeting with Beara and Popovic at the Zvornik Brigade Command, that he then attended -- that Drago Nikolic attended this meeting, during which he was informed of a number of prisoners about to arrive, and he was asked to accommodate them in schools previously identified, such as the Kula school. Considering that the 1st Battalion had already been informed by telegram of the arrival of prisoners, coming out of this meeting Drago Nikolic picks up the phone, calls the security officer from the 1st Battalion to suggest to him -- not to order him, but to suggest to him, Whatever your commander decided, or, Whoever your commander decided to send to the Kula school, let's avoid any problems with the local population. You should go there because your house is located close to the school and you know the area. Then Drago Nikolic meets with his driver. He informs his driver of what he has been told during this meeting. He expresses his dissatisfaction, without reserve, and they drive to Hotel Vidikovac, where sometime later the convoy of prisoners arrives. This scenario, Mr. President, is supported by the evidence in a much stronger way than the inference the Prosecution would like you to draw. The inference the Prosecution is asking you to draw is simply a bridge too far. That being said, we're not blind to the evidence, as I said yesterday, at some point Drago Nikolic found out that prisoners taken to Orahovac school were being killed. That is a given. As argued in our final trial brief, this took place, at the earliest, when Drago Nikolic returned to the Orahovac school in the early evening and, from there, drove to the IKM with his driver, Bircakovic. For purpose of his knowledge of the common purpose, however, even when Drago Nikolic found out that prisoners were being killed, what matters is that he did -- that did not provide him with the knowledge of the common purpose of the alleged JCE to kill all the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. This, he never learned, and there is no evidence that he did, not even when he was allegedly close to the Petkovci school in the afternoon of 14 July or when he saw 40 to 50 bodies driving by the water point with Bircakovic that night. The evidence provided, of course, by Witness PW-101, as mentioned earlier, cannot be attributed weight, and it simply cannot be concluded that Drago Nikolic was present at the execution site that night. In these circumstances, we respectfully submit that it must be concluded that he was not a member of the alleged JCE, the purpose of which was to kill all able-bodied men from Srebrenica. Does that mean that he was not involved in any way in what happened in Orahovac on 14 July? Of course not, Mr. President. I said that at the beginning of these closing arguments. The evidence reveals that Drago Nikolic was close enough to the events which took place in Orahovac to possibly incur some individual criminal responsibility. Consequently, I will now address the Prosecution's arguments, in part Roman XII of the Prosecution's final brief, the title of which is "Individual Criminal Responsibility of Drago Nikolic Under Article 7(1) of the Statute." The best way to do this, Mr. President, is to refer to the overview of the Prosecution's case against Drago Nikolic found in section -- I was supposed to make something funny here, CCXIII or III of the Prosecution's final brief. I don't know who had the idea to use Roman numerals for these sections, but it was quite a feat to make my way through the Prosecution's brief. At paragraph 2600, the Prosecution submits that the involvement of Drago Nikolic in the murder operation began when he was contacted by Vujadin Popovic and asked to make preparations for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're going too fast, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reporter is not catching up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise. As argued by my colleague Zivanovic and as explained earlier, it is our submission, Mr. President, that this telephone conversation between Popovic and Drago Nikolic never took place. It follows that the very foundation of the alleged telephone conversation between Dragan Obrenovic and Drago Nikolic is inexistent. Consequently, without the alleged information coming from Popovic, there is no reason for Obrenovic to call -- sorry, for Drago Nikolic to call Obrenovic at that time. It is thus evident that this part of Obrenovic's statement of facts is nothing but a fabrication. So Drago Nikolic, of course, if that conversation did not take place, was not authorised to leave his post at the IKM that evening, nor was he authorised to use Jasikovac and five or six MPs unfit for combat for the purpose of assisting Beara and Popovic with the POWs. Moreover, the evidence reveals that Jasikovac is the one who gave the orders for MPs to go to Orahovac; Stevo Kostic transcript 26003. So how did this take place? Well, consider the following, Mr. President: There is no evidence that Jasikovac was in the field that night. It would have been illogical for Obrenovic to withdraw the commander of the military police in the field at this critical time. The tactical intercept used by the Prosecution, that is, P2232, contains no reference to a conversation involving Jasikovac. If Obrenovic had received instructions regarding the -- sorry. Obrenovic had received instructions regarding the detention of members captured from the column in the early afternoon; that is P45. Obrenovic did not inform the duty officer, Sreten Milosevic, of what was going on. Drago Nikolic was at the IKM, and he was of no immediate assistance to Obrenovic. Considering that the time at which Obrenovic left the Zvornik Brigade Command that night is after the time the military policemen would have left to Orahovac, the logical conclusion, Mr. President, is that Obrenovic must have received personally the information that a group of prisoners would be sent to Orahovac. He never spoke to Drago Nikolic about this. He personally gave the order to Jasikovac to take the members of the military police who were available at Standard not because they were unfit, but because that was their place of duty that night, to go to Orahovac and prepare the school. In his statement of facts, Obrenovic lied about the involvement of Drago Nikolic because the Prosecution put pressure on him to fill in the gap in its evidence and because, of course, admitting his true responsibility in these events would have meant a much higher sentence recommendation. The next allegation in the Prosecution's overview is at paragraph 2601, that Drago Nikolic oversaw the deployment of MPs and the detention of prisoners who arrived at Orahovac that night, and of course the Prosecution says knowing that they would be murdered, but I've dealt with that already. Strikingly, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. Once again, strikingly, the Prosecution omitted in its overview the alleged visit of Momir Nikolic at the IKM that night. The reason for this is obvious, as mentioned in our brief. The Prosecution knows that Momir Nikolic lied, and before the Trial Chamber decided to call him as a witness in this case, they had given up on trying to rely on his evidence. There is no evidence, Mr. President, that Drago Nikolic was informed on 13 July that prisoners would be murdered in the Zvornik area. There is also no evidence that Drago Nikolic -- that Drago Nikolic, sorry, was at the Orahovac school during the evening or night of 13 to 14 July. As mentioned earlier, the testimony of PW-143, the only one who would maybe have seen Drago Nikolic at the Orahovac school, cannot be given any weight. Another missing element in the Prosecution's overview is the alleged replacement of Drago Nikolic by Galic that night. It is significant in this regard that the Prosecution did not prove or attempt to prove, for that matter, the whereabouts of Drago Nikolic that night if he had been replaced at the IKM, contrary to the evidence and our arguments. Moreover, the Prosecution refers to the testimony of Bircakovic. The Prosecution does not dispute the fact that he was ordered by Trbic to pick up Drago Nikolic at the IKM on the morning of 14 July and that he did so. That's final brief of Prosecution paragraph 654/655. If Bircakovic went to the IKM to pick up Drago Nikolic on 14 July, in the morning, then where was Galic? These are powerful indicators that Drago Nikolic was never replaced at the IKM that night. The Prosecution overview, paragraph 2602, the meeting with Beara and Popovic, I've dealt with that already. The order to the 1st Battalion -- to the security officer of the 1st Battalion, that's 2603, I've dealt with that. The Prosecution overview 2604, that the day of 14 July Drago Nikolic oversaw the detention of prisoners at Orahovac, there's no evidence that he coordinated anything at Orahovac. The only witness who says this is PW-101, and his evidence is not worthy of belief. We have to consider the evidence provided by MPs about how many times Drago Nikolic was at Orahovac that day. Of course, the Prosecution takes all the times that all the military policemen say that Drago Nikolic was there, and conclude that he was there many times. It's just different times for those two events that have been proven. Drago Nikolic was there twice. More importantly, there is no evidence that the military police from the Zvornik Brigade blindfolded the prisoners and placed them on trucks. The evidence reveals that some members from the Bratunac Brigade came in. The Prosecution did not even investigate that. We provided the Prosecution with the indictment that exists against members of the Bratunac Brigade. That is 3D133. They never looked into that. They weren't interested in finding out who was blindfolding the prisoners, who was putting them on the truck. They weren't interested in that. They knew, from the testimony of the victims, that persons wearing red berets were involved in these events. Did they try and go and look to Bratunac Red Beret? My colleague said it's a very famous unit who may have been involved in the executions. They did not look into that. Prosecution overview 2607 or 2606, that Drago was present at the execution site, I have dealt with that already. 2607. He did not place any phone calls to Acimovic. That's established, and I've dealt with that. 2608. Now we get into pure speculation, an alleged meeting between Drago Nikolic and Beara at the Zvornik Brigade Command on 15 July. Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we deal with that after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've been informed by the Registrar that according to the two and a half hours which had been allocated or allotted, sorry, to the Nikolic Defence team, we have 15 minutes left. Mr. President, I ask for your indulgence, and I can say that we can complete our submissions in 40 minutes. That would be 25 minutes' additional time, and we will complete our submissions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Before the break ended, I was addressing the Prosecution overview, and I was at paragraph 2610, and I -- 2611, sorry. Sorry, I apologise. I was at 2608 and telling you that a meeting with Beara and Popovic at the Zvornik Brigade Command on the 15 July is nothing but speculation. Many witnesses testified on what happened on the 15th July, in the morning. Nobody -- no evidence -- no one mentioned the presence of Beara at the Zvornik Brigade Command. Even Witness Pandurevic, who testified and explained everything that happened when he returned to the Zvornik Brigade Command, and despite the fact that his theory, that Beara had taken over the Zvornik Brigade Command, he never even mentioned that Beara was there on 15 July, in the morning. Mr. President, I move on to 2609, the fact that the Prosecution says that Drago Nikolic went with Trbic to Rocevic school. Simply looking at the time, it's not possible. The Prosecution would like you to believe that Drago Nikolic was everywhere at the same time, that he was on duty that morning as of 11.45, that he was in the morning, according to the testimony of Mico Gavric, he met with persons at the Zvornik Brigade Command in the morning. And then the Prosecution would like to place him at the Rocevic school. If you look at the testimony of Witness PW-165 carefully, there is no weight that can be attributed to this allegation or it simply has not been proved. The Prosecution again continues in its speculation at 2610, saying that because Drago Nikolic was on duty that morning, that's the very early morning, he gets a request for ammunition from the 1st Battalion, that this is sufficient to put Drago Nikolic on knowledge about what is happening at the 1st Battalion and that people will be killed there that day. This is simply an inference which cannot be drawn beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution continues by saying that Drago Nikolic was involved in the murder of the four Branjevo Farm survivors. We address that. The sole evidence on the record on this issue comes from Witness PW-168, and it cannot be attributed any probative value. As for the fact that Drago Nikolic was not involved in the burial, again, the sole evidence on the record is Witness PW-168. There is an intercept about the reburials, but this intercept, in our view, can only be interpreted with the benefit going to Drago Nikolic, that he was not involved in the reburials. It is also significant, regarding the reburials, that Drago Nikolic, according to the evidence on the record, was away when these reburials took place. Finally, I need to address, Mr. President, a very important topic, which is the fact that it appears that the Prosecution has withdrawn or given up leading evidence or arguing that Drago Nikolic was responsible for what happened to the patients from the Milici hospital who were transferred to the Zvornik Brigade. This was an allegation which was in the indictment against Drago Nikolic. It was also mentioned in the Prosecution pre-trial brief, although I do not have the reference. And to the best of my recollection, the Prosecution also mentioned this in its opening statement. However, there is no mention whatsoever, in the Prosecution final trial brief, that Drago Nikolic is in any way involved in the disappearance or murder of the patients taken from Milici hospital. I expected that in oral arguments the Prosecution would make a correction to that effect. It has not done so. Accordingly, Mr. President, the only conclusion which can be drawn immediately, actually, that Drago Nikolic was not involved in what happened to the patients from the Milici hospital transferred to Zvornik. I take this opportunity to mention one mistake I did earlier on, when I was referring to the testimony of Witness Stojkic. I said that he testified coming back with the tank company. That is not correct. He did not testify to that effect, so that's a mistake and I apologise for this mistake. It's something that we argued in the brief, that he came back with the tank company, but he never said that. He simply said that he returned on 13 July. I now move to Count 1, genocide. Of course, our position is that no genocide was committed, and even if genocide was committed, that Drago Nikolic incurs no individual criminal responsibility for genocide. The Appeals Chamber has already held previously, in the Krstic case, that a genocide was committed in Srebrenica. However, this is a factual conclusion which is not binding on this Trial Chamber. This Trial Chamber must decide if a genocide was committed in Srebrenica on the basis of the evidence in this case, not in previous cases. When we compare the evidence led in the Krstic case with the evidence led in this case, there are huge differences. We know much more information today that was not known to the Appeals Chamber or to the Trial Chamber in the Krstic case. Using the same line of reasoning as the Appeals Chamber did in the Krstic case, and we're applying it to the evidence in this case, it is our submission that it was not genocide. So going straight to the Prosecution's allegation, well, they change, of course, their view from the indictment until their final trial brief. There used to be four components to the alleged genocide; now there's only two. They drop the reburials and they drop the opportunistic killings as being part or components of the alleged genocide. Now, what they say in the final trial brief is that the genocide is made up of the two joint criminal enterprise: One, to kill all the able-bodied men; and, two, to forcibly transfer the population from Srebrenica and Zepa enclave. Just the wording they use, Mr. President, shows that my previous submission is correct, in the sense that when they talk about killing all the able-bodied men, and they make a separation between that and the population from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, shows that the men were not forcibly transferred. Something different happened to the men, not forcible transfer. Mr. President, there are obvious problems with the alleged joint criminal enterprise to kill all the able-bodied men from Srebrenica. First of all, it is undisputed that not all the able-bodied men from Srebrenica were, in fact, killed, so the common purpose of the alleged JCE was not achieved. Then, based on the evidence as a whole, including forensic evidence and the demographic evidence, it simply cannot be concluded beyond a reasonable doubt that more than 7.000 Muslim men from Srebrenica were killed as a result of the crimes forming the basis of this indictment. Of course, none of the Defence teams will be able to use an hour to make submissions just on this specific topic, as the Prosecution was able to do, but it doesn't matter, because our submissions and our brief clearly show that beyond a reasonable doubt the maximum number of persons who have been killed as a result of the crimes committed in this case does not exceed 3.000. Secondly and most importantly, in respect of the JCE to kill all the able-bodied men, there are many counter-indications that the events which took place in Eastern Bosnia in July 1995 reflect a genocidal intent. One counter-indicator is that the men who were killed while travelling with the column going to Tuzla were killed as a result of legitimate combat activities, which negates the proposition that they were killed for the purpose of destroying, in whole or in part, the Bosnian Muslim group, as such. The Prosecution conceded on this that no less than 70 to 73 per cent of those killed appear on the ABiH records. Now, that's significant. 73 per cent of the members of the column were on ABiH records, so they were actually aiming and they were actually fighting soldiers, not committing -- not attempting to destroy the Bosnian Muslim population, as such. Another counter-indicator is the fact that a large number of men from Srebrenica were allowed to link up with the 2nd Corps. The reason why they were let through, whether it is because they were too strong or whether it is because it was to avoid a carnage on both sides, is irrelevant. The fact is that they were let through, without fighting, shows that there was no intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Bosnian Muslim group, as such. The orders issued from the Main Staff down, to prevent these men from linking up with the 2nd Corps of the ABiH, not to kill them, shows that there was no intent to kill the able-bodied men. Another counter-indicator. Contrary to the Appeal Chamber findings in the Krstic case, the military-able men from Zepa, according to the evidence in this case, were under the control of the VRS, yet no genocidal acts were committed against them. Another counter-indicator is the holding of the Darfur Commission which held that the killing of young men selectively within the population does not demonstrate genocidal intent. This is paragraph 513 of the Darfur report. Another counter-indicator is the fact that prisoners who were held at the Kula school were transferred in the custody of military police from the East Bosnia Corps and transferred away from the area of Zvornik. They were taken to Batkovici. This shows that there was no intent to kill or to destroy, in whole or in part, the Bosnian Muslim group. I refer to Novica Simic at transcript 28567/28569. What I referred to earlier also, the chaos that was in Bratunac on the 13th of July, shows that there were -- there was no genocidal plan. Of course there was some killing, of course there were some crimes, and of course they were atrocious, but there was never that intent in that area at the time. Lastly, my colleague said during his oral argument - that's at transcript 34276 - that what happened in Srebrenica was ethnic cleansing. Well, I'm not going to say I agree, but what I'll say is that this is an admission by the Prosecution that it was not genocide. Ethnic cleansing is not genocide. What happened in July 1995 is that the VRS was looking for a piece of land to be in a good position to negotiate, as the ABiH was doing -- trying to fight in Sarajevo and as the Croats were doing, fighting for Operation Storm also in July 1995, not to destroy, in whole or in part, the Bosnian Muslim group, as such. Mr. President, there are also obvious problems with the alleged JCE to force out the Muslim population in respect of genocidal intent. One of these problems was illustrated by the holding of the Darfur Commission presided by no other than Antonio Cassese. He said that forcible transfer is actually a counter-indication of genocidal intent; paragraph 515 of the Darfur report. Of course, the fact that people are forced to move to another location, albeit as a result of a crime, does not display intent or genocidal intent. It actually supports the proposition that the physical or biological destruction of the group was not the aim. An additional problem is again the holding of the Darfur Commission, which is supported by the fact that two of the co-accused in this case, although they are charged with forcible transfer, are not charged with genocide. This shows that the Prosecution's understanding that being a member of the JCE to force out the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, if it was proved, of course, does not entail having genocidal intent. That's a significant, again, admission on the Prosecution's side. Lastly and thirdly -- and thirdly, there is even a more important problem, which is that even if the actions taken to further both alleged JCEs, taken together, that would not demonstrate genocidal intent, as explained again in the Darfur report. This is what the commission concluded: "Holding that the attackers did not entertain genocidal intent, as their intent was to murder all those men they considered as rebels, as well as forcibly expel the whole population as to vacate the villages and prevent rebels from hiding among or getting support from the local population." For all these reasons, there was no genocide committed in the area of Srebrenica. Furthermore, even if the Trial Chamber was to conclude that genocide was committed, the Prosecution failed to prove that Drago Nikolic had the required mens rea. The Prosecution argues that genocidal plan for Srebrenica evolved from policy directives and subsequent decisions of members of the RS and VRS leadership. It is significant that Drago Nikolic was not aware of these policies and these subsequent decisions. The Prosecution then says that genocidal plan culminated in both JCEs. Well, as we argued, Drago Nikolic was not a member of either alleged joint criminal enterprise. It must also be noted that the central role played by Drago Nikolic in the crimes committed in July 1995, as alleged by the Prosecution, simply has not been proved. Clearly, the acts and conduct of Drago Nikolic during the period from 12 to 17 July, coupled with his limited knowledge of any goals pursued by the RS and DRS leadership, do not support the conclusion that he harboured genocidal intent. The Prosecution goes on to argue that Drago Nikolic intent to commit genocide is evidenced by his personal use of derogatory language. Well, we know that the Appeals Chamber clearly held that such charge language is commonplace during wartime, and therefore no weight may be attached to it in establishing genocidal intent. Finally, the Prosecution argues that Drago Nikolic genocidal intent may be inferred from the high level of planning and coordination which went into the murder operation, and the systematic nature in which the bodies were -- of the murdered Muslims were buried and then reburied. The Prosecution has failed to prove that Drago Nikolic would have contributed to the alleged high-level planning and coordination. Drago Nikolic did not harbour the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Bosnian Muslim group, as such. The Prosecution -- I move now to the last topic quickly, which is conspiracy to commit genocide. I note, for the record, that there's almost nothing about this Count number 2 in the Prosecution final brief. I refer to our arguments, the first one being that the Prosecution simply mixes things up or confuses conspiracy to commit genocide with joint criminal enterprise. One is a mode of liability; one is a crime. And during his oral submissions, my colleague from the Prosecution, Mitchell, said that Drago became a member of the conspiracy later on. That doesn't exist. It is possible for an individual to ultimately become a member of a joint criminal enterprise once he's made aware of the common purpose, and he intends to further it, and he significantly contributes to it, but the conspiracy itself is finished by then. Conspiracy -- you cannot buy into a conspiracy at a later point. Even if the Trial Chamber would find that the crime of conspiracy to commit genocide was committed in Eastern Bosnia in July 1995, contrary to our arguments, the evidence clearly establishes that Drago Nikolic does not incur liability because to be a member of the conspiracy you need to have genocidal intent, and Drago Nikolic did not have genocidal intent. Finally, with respect to persecutions, I refer the Trial Chamber to the arguments in our brief, and once again I note that the Prosecution has not even attempted to properly explain or prove -- or explain how each of the co-accused in this case had the necessary discriminatory intent. What was done in July 1995, by whoever it was done, was not done because they were Muslims, because the victims were Muslims. It was done because it was the enemy. It was done to gain territory. There was no persecutions, as alleged by the Prosecution. On this, Mr. President, I will hand over to my colleague, who will now address with respect to sentencing considerations and final remarks. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. A lot has been said over the last three years and during our oral submissions, and therefore I will only address the mitigating and aggravating circumstances relating to the sentences and the character of Mr. Nikolic as stated in the Prosecution brief and its closing arguments. In his closing argument of 2nd September 2009, on transcript pages 34046 and 3407 [as interpreted], Mr. McCloskey pointed out three things are necessary to prove the guilt of the accused -- excuse me just for a second. I'm sorry, my LiveNote is blocked -- which is that the accused consciously disregarded their duty, that the accused did not sabotage the crime or help the victims, and that the accused decided to participate in the crimes. Firstly, I'm not going to repeat the fact that Drago Nikolic, as the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade, did not have any responsibilities and powers regarding the prisoners of war. Therefore, the Prosecution did not prove that Drago Nikolic disregarded his duties. Secondly, the Prosecution has not charged Drago Nikolic for command responsibility or on the basis of command responsibility, and therefore cannot accuse him of failing to prevent crimes at the end of the trial. And, finally, the Prosecution did not adduce evidence, as my colleague pointed out, that Drago Nikolic was aware of the common plans, that he intended to further the common plans, and that he had significantly contributed to the common plans, and that he had the required intent for the crimes included in the JCE. Drago Nikolic was taken aback by the events of surprise and scope and speed in Zvornik on the 14th of July 1995. It has been said at one point in time Drago Nikolic found out and realised that prisoners of war, who had been brought to Orahovac, had been executed. That happened in the evening of the 14th of July, 1995. Drago Nikolic was in the proximity of the school in Orahovac and Petkovci, but he never went to Pilica or Rocevic during the critical events. It is necessary to highlight that what took place on the 14th of July is important for establishing his responsibility. What is even more important is to establish what Drago Nikolic could have done; in other words, what his real options were, having in mind his rank, his position, his ability to influence the events, the overwhelming nature of what was happening, the scope of the operations, and the rank and authority of all other officers who were involved. The facts in this case show that Drago Nikolic could not have influenced in any way the decision to bring the prisoners of war to the territory of Zvornik. He learned about his arrival only upon their arrival. He could not have prevented the prisoners being put up in schools. He could not have secured food and water for them, nor could he have secretly called a TV station, as suggested by the Prosecution in its final brief at paragraph 2715. Briefly, his possibilities were considerably limited. Also, Mr. President, I would like to address the aggravating circumstances as listed by the Prosecution in their final brief at paragraphs 2816 to 2827. The Prosecution claims that the scope of the crimes, the number of victims, and the vulnerability and status of the victims are aggravating circumstances. Your Honours, these elements cannot be treated as aggravating circumstances, as they have already been incorporated in the definition of the crimes that the accused has been charged with, including Drago Nikolic. This has been argued in the Blagojevic and Jokic judgement, paragraphs 841 and 843. Secondly, the Prosecution's claims, in paragraphs of their final brief 2822 to 2825, that Drago Nikolic's high rank and position in the brigade are aggravating circumstances. However, as indicated already, Your Honours, Drago Nikolic was a second lieutenant, which is the lowest possible rank for an officer, as explained in our final brief in paragraphs 412 to 415. His position in the brigade can be seen from the testimony of PW-104, who said that Drago Nikolic, as a second lieutenant, did not have any importance; transcript page 8018. He certainly did not hold the high rank as claimed by the Prosecution, nor the authority. Thirdly, in the Prosecution's view, in paragraphs 2826 to 2827, the willing participation of Drago Nikolic in the crimes also constitutes an aggravated circumstance. In our final brief, as well as in our closing arguments, the Defence strongly rejects the Prosecution's claims in this respect. Drago Nikolic was drawn into the whirlwind of events without ever being asked whether he was willing to do that or not. Mr. President, in this respect I would like to draw a parallel with Dragan Jokic, who was sentenced by this Tribunal on the basis of the same events. In paragraph 836 of the Blagojevic and Jokic judgement, the Trial Chamber took account of the limited involvement of Dragan Jokic and his low rank were the key factors in determining the sentence. As has already been said, the involvement of Drago Nikolic in these events was also very limited. He was not a member of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, even though he bears part of the responsibility because of his proximity to the events. He was a second lieutenant, which is the lowest rank for an officer, and he did not have the authority of a superior officer. Mr. President, I respectfully draw the Trial Chamber's attention to our arguments in relation to the character of Drago Nikolic in paragraphs 396 to 421 of our final brief. I also respectfully recall the testimonies of witnesses who appeared before this Trial Chamber to testify about the character of Drago Nikolic and the events of July 1995,

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (redacted). The evidence before this Trial Chamber relating to his character show that he is a man who never expressed hatred or inter-ethnic intolerance, who conscientiously discharged his duties, who respected his superior officers. He grew up in the spirit of tolerance, which is confirmed by the current relationships in his family, as indicated in our final brief in paragraph 490. Finally, Mr. President, I call upon the Trial Chamber to take into account the character and the limited involvement of Drago Nikolic, as opposed to other individuals who were involved in these events. In relation to this, I would like to say one thing. Drago Nikolic did not participate in the events as presented by the Prosecution, and he definitely is not the kind of person that the Prosecution would like to portray him to be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Judge Kwon, any questions? Judge Stole? Judge Prost?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon, I have a couple of questions for you. Back at the beginning of your submissions, Mr. Bourgon, and it's specifically page 6, line 12, you were discussing -- and perhaps out of an abundance of caution, because this was in private session, we should go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: This is an argument that was made by both you and Mr. Ostojic as well made several references in this regard, and I simply want to be clear as to your proposition here. You have pointed to particular witnesses that the Prosecution, for whatever reason, chose not to call in this case, and what I'd like to know is whether you're suggesting there is any form of inference that this Trial Chamber can derive from the failure of the Prosecution to call particular witnesses. And if that is your proposition, that we can draw a negative inference, I'd like to know what authority there is in support of that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. To put it bluntly, there is no negative inference that can be drawn from the fact that the Prosecution did not call a witness. That's this -- if this is what came from what my argument looked like, it was not what was intended. What is intended, however, is to support what my colleague from the Prosecution said was inappropriate in the Borovcanin final brief. He argued that it was improper to suggest that it's unsafe to make inferences on the basis of evidence when you know that evidence is missing. So it's not drawing a negative inference about the Prosecution's conduct. It's the fact that when the time will come for the Trial Chamber to draw an inference, if there is information that is missing, if there is information that would have assisted the Trial Chamber in leaning one way or another, then definitely the benefit must go to the accused, and that inference cannot be drawn. To use an example, the example I use is, of course: Who ordered the military police to go to Orahovac on the evening of 13 July? There is evidence that Jasikovac ordered the military police to go to Orahovac. That -- there is direct evidence about this by some witnesses; namely, Stevo Kostic. However, the involvement of PW-168 into how and who told Jasikovac to go to Orahovac, the Trial Chamber will have to make an inference. Because Jasikovac was not called as a witness and could have been called, then there might be there is some critical information missing. And because that critical information is missing, then the Trial Chamber will have to make an inference that -- where the doubt will benefit to the accused. And the accused in this case is a man who we say never called Dragan Obrenovic that night to report to him information he would have received from Popovic. So the missing information will prevent the Trial Chamber from drawing, in certain circumstances, negative inferences against the accused. That's what we're saying, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. I have now just two legal questions for you, Mr. Bourgon. I have, of course, read carefully the arguments outlined in the brief on these various issues, so my question on forcible transfer is quite limited, but I'd like to know, with respect particularly to the individuals -- the men separated at Potocari, is it your proposition that were an army to take control of a town, it would be lawful -- a town where there has been allegations of opposition army members being present in that town, would it be lawful for them to, upon entering the town, to go to every house and take into custody every able-bodied man, and place all those men onto buses and move them out of that town? Is it your proposition that where there is an allegation, a suggestion, that the armed forces of the opposition have been present in the town, that it's lawful to take that action and it doesn't constitute forcible transfer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My answer is "yes," Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
